summary: This memo describes use cases, requirements, and protocol extensions for using the SDP offer/answer model to set up audio and video media over circuit-switched bearers in the PSTN.

eli5.summary: This lets a modern call setup message say to use an ordinary phone line for sound and pictures.

questions: sdp for circuit-switched audio and video
how does sdp negotiate a pstn audio stream
what is the pstn nettype in sdp
how does an endpoint match a phone call to an sdp session
subtitle: How SDP offer/answer can set up an audio or video stream over an ordinary phone-network call while the signaling runs over IP.

tldr.problem: Sometimes two devices that signal over IP would rather carry voice or video over a circuit-switched phone-network bearer, for example when the radio link is poor for real-time media. SDP had no way to describe such a stream or to tie an incoming phone call to the IP session.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds a PSTN network type, an E164 address type and a PSTN protocol type to SDP, plus a cs-correlation attribute that carries an identifier (caller ID, User-User Information Element, DTMF digits, or a human decision) so the receiver can recognise the matching call. The active or passive role is negotiated with the setup attribute from RFC 4145.
tldr.outcome: Endpoints can negotiate a circuit-switched audio or video stream in a normal offer/answer exchange and recognise the resulting phone call as part of the session. The RFC admits the correlation hints are not guaranteed to survive the phone network.

today: RFC 7195 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2014. The metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Use a Phone Bearer for a Session
sections.content:
The Session Description Protocol (SDP) normally describes media carried over RTP, and is commonly carried in SIP messages using the offer/answer model of RFC 3264. RFC 7195 covers a different case: the session signaling stays on IP, but the audio or video travels over a circuit-switched bearer in the Public Switched Telephone Network (PSTN).

The main scenario is two mobile devices with both circuit-switched and packet-switched access over a low-bandwidth radio bearer. That bearer may be poor for real-time media, so a circuit-switched call gives better perceived quality. Setting up the IP session also lets the endpoints negotiate other media that is not sensitive to jitter and delay, such as text messaging or presence. Later, a device that moves into range of a high-bandwidth bearer such as a WLAN can renegotiate and move the media over.

Other use cases are endpoints whose circuit-switched and packet-switched sides support different codecs, and third party call control, where session setup is faster when the PSTN bearer is described along with codecs. The RFC addresses only PSTN circuit-switched bearers, not a generic circuit-switched network, and it relies on a PSTN call signaling protocol such as ITU-T Q.931 or 3GPP TS 24.008.
sections.eli5: Sometimes the internet connection is too shaky for a good chat, but a regular phone call sounds fine. This lets two devices use the internet to arrange things and the phone line to do the talking.

sections.title: Requirements and Overview
sections.content:
The RFC lists seven requirements. A mechanism MUST exist to negotiate a circuit-switched audio or video stream, combine it with other streams such as text messaging, and negotiate the direction in which the bearer is set up. It MUST be independent of the access type (ISDN, GSM and so on). It MUST help an endpoint correlate an incoming circuit-switched call with the one negotiated in SDP, and where programmatic correlation is impossible a human user may do it. Finally, endpoints MUST be able to advertise different codec lists for the circuit-switched stream than for a packet-switched one, or advertise no codec list at all.

The solution extends SDP with a new network type (PSTN) and a new protocol type (PSTN) for the c= and m= lines. Because circuit-switched bearers are connection-oriented, it reuses the connection-oriented extensions of RFC 4145 to decide who is the active and who is the passive side.

In the basic flow, Endpoint A sends an offer describing PSTN audio. Endpoint B answers, and the two agree on which side places the call. In the RFC's example B becomes active and calls A. A recognises the call as belonging to the session and accepts it. To reject the stream, B sets its port to zero as RFC 3264 specifies. If B does not understand attributes from this document, it ignores them as RFC 4566 specifies.
sections.eli5: The rules say the plan must work for any kind of phone network, let you add a chat alongside the call, and let you tell which incoming call belongs to the plan. Then the two devices agree who will do the dialing.

sections.title: New SDP Values for Connection and Media Lines
sections.content:
In the c= line, the network type is PSTN and the new address type is E164, meaning the connection address is an international E.164 telephone number. The number is written with a leading +, using the global-number-digits form from RFC 3966. If the endpoint does not know its own number, the address is a dash, because the field must not be omitted. Example: c=PSTN E164 +441134960123. The RFC notes that this E164 address type is distinct from the E.164 type defined in RFC 3108 and must not be used with the PSTN network type.

In the m= line, the media is audio or video and the protocol is PSTN. A circuit-switched bearer has no port, so the port SHOULD be the discard port value 9 and MUST be ignored on reception. A port of zero keeps its RFC 3264 meaning: offered but not to be used, or rejected in an answer.

The format field reuses RTP payload type numbers from RFC 3551 to list the codecs available over the bearer, in priority order, for example m=audio 9 PSTN 3 0 8. If the endpoint cannot determine the available codecs, it MUST put a single dash there: m=audio 9 PSTN -.

The o= line keeps the IP address of the signaling source, since SDP itself is still carried over IP. The p= line is not used for the connection address.
sections.eli5: It adds new words to the SDP vocabulary: "this is a phone line" and "here is the phone number". If you do not know your own number or the voice format, you write a dash, which means unknown.

sections.title: Correlating the Phone Call with the Session
sections.content:
When a phone call arrives, the endpoint needs to know whether it belongs to the SDP session, so it does not ring as an unrelated call. All mechanisms share one idea: some unique information is sent in SDP and in the circuit-switched signaling. If the two match, the call is part of the session. They are announced in a media-level cs-correlation attribute, at most once per media description.

  • callerid: the international E.164 number is sent in SDP and must match the Calling Party Number Information Element in the call setup. The RFC warns the number may be unknown, hidden by privacy or operator policy, or formatted differently, so implementations should consider only some of the rightmost digits.
  • uuie: a value is sent in SDP and in the User-User Information Element of the call setup. It starts with the Protocol Discriminator octet, then the User Information octets, is base 16 encoded, and must have an even number of hex digits. That element has a maximum size of 35 or 131 octets, depending on the message and network settings.
  • dtmf: a digit sequence is sent in SDP, and the caller sends the same digits as DTMF tones once the bearer is established. The RFC suggests 5 to 10 digits as a good compromise.
  • external: no value. The decision is left to something outside the protocol, typically the human user, who accepts or rejects the call.

Example attribute lines: a=cs-correlation:callerid:+441134960123 and a=cs-correlation:uuie:56A390F3D2B7310023. New mechanisms can be registered with the policy Specification Required, and an unknown value MUST be treated as unsupported.

None of these is guaranteed to work, because they need support from the phone network. A single positive indication from any mechanism SHOULD be taken as showing the call belongs to the session. If a mechanism was agreed but a call arrives with no correlation information, the endpoint checks whether external was also negotiated. If so, the human decides. If not, the call is treated as unrelated.
sections.eli5: It is like a secret handshake for phone calls. You agree beforehand that the call will show a certain number, carry a certain code, or start with certain button presses, so you can tell it is the call you were waiting for. If the handshake fails, a person can decide.

sections.title: Offer/Answer Procedures and Roles
sections.content:
To prevent both sides dialing at once, the direction of bearer setup MUST be negotiated. The RFC reuses the setup attribute of RFC 4145 (values active, passive, actpass and holdconn) and the connection attribute (new or existing). The active party is the one that places the circuit-switched call.

The offer. The offerer sets c= to PSTN E164 with its own number if known (otherwise a dash), sets m= as above, and includes one cs-correlation line listing the mechanisms it supports. If it is willing to be active it fills in values for callerid, uuie and dtmf, and never a value for external. If it can only be passive it lists mechanisms without values. An offerer that does not know its number MUST set setup to active, and the first offer MUST use connection:new.

The answer. An answerer that cannot or will not use circuit-switched media sets the port to zero. If the offerer can only be active, the answerer must be passive (and know its own number) or reject. If the offerer can only be passive, the answerer must be active, which requires the offerer's number in the c= line. If the offerer can be either and gave its number, the answerer SHOULD be active. The answer keeps only mechanisms from the offer, and only an active answerer adds values. An offer with a dash as the payload type should be accepted with dash in the answer, and naming a codec in the answer is NOT RECOMMENDED.

After the exchange. The active party extracts the E.164 number from the c= line, places the call, and sets the Calling Party Number, User-User Information Element or DTMF digits as agreed. The passive party compares what arrives with the SDP values. An offerer MUST NOT accept an incoming call before it has received the answer. If an active answerer then finds the call cannot be established, it MUST send a new offer removing the stream by setting the port to zero.

Changes later. To reuse a bearer, set connection to existing. Setting the port to zero removes the media and the bearer must be terminated. To drop and re-establish, remove the media first, then re-offer with connection:new.
sections.eli5: First the two sides agree who will place the phone call. Whoever calls shares the code, and whoever answers checks the code. If the call cannot go through, they tell each other so that both know the plan changed.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 4566 and RFC 3264 apply. In addition, an attacker who copies a correlation identifier and places a call while the endpoint is expecting one may hijack the circuit-switched bearer. The RFC notes this is not specific to its mechanisms; Caller ID spoofing is a well-known PSTN attack. It also warns that media protection such as SRTP used on the IP side is not available in the circuit-switched domain.

Phone numbers are sensitive. Implementations should respect the caller's calling line identification preferences, such as CLIR in GSM, by restricting the number in the c= line, or prompt the user that the number may be sent. To protect SDP carried in SIP, follow the mechanisms of RFC 3261.

An attacker could also try to make an endpoint dial a number, perhaps a premium-rate one. Endpoints MUST authenticate and trust remote users who try to remain passive. Local policies against active calls to certain numbers (for example international, premium and long distance) are RECOMMENDED, and asking the user for consent before the endpoint initiates a call is strongly RECOMMENDED.
sections.eli5: A trickster might copy the secret handshake or try to make your phone dial an expensive number. So the rules say to check who you trust, avoid dialing costly numbers by default, and ask the owner first.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the media-level attribute cs-correlation, with the long-form name PSTN Correlation Identifier. It created a subregistry of its values under the SDP Parameters registry, with initial values callerid, uuie, dtmf and external. New values use the Specification Required policy.

IANA also registered the nettype value PSTN, the addrtype value E164 (defined only in the context of the PSTN network type) and the proto value PSTN, all pointing to RFC 7195.
sections.eli5: The new words were added to the official list of SDP words so that nobody else uses them for something different.

messages.label: SDP offer (PSTN audio)
messages.note: Describes audio over a circuit-switched bearer.

messages.label: SDP answer (PSTN audio)
messages.note: B takes the active role in the example.

messages.label: PSTN call setup
messages.note: A correlates the call with the session, then media flows over the PSTN bearer.

items.label: Caller ID
items.desc: E.164 number matched against the Calling Party Number Information Element.

items.label: User-User Information Element
items.desc: Hex-encoded value matched against the UUIE in the call setup.

items.label: DTMF digits
items.desc: Digit sequence sent as DTMF tones after the bearer is established.

items.label: External
items.desc: No value; the human user or other external means decides.

data.title: SDP offer with PSTN audio
data.code:
v=0
o=alice 2890844526 2890842807 IN IP4 192.0.2.5
s=
t=0 0
m=audio 9 PSTN -
c=PSTN E164 +441134960123
a=setup:actpass
a=connection:new
a=cs-correlation:callerid:+441134960123 \
  uuie:56A390F3D2B7310023 external
